The '''FLLA World Cup''', sometimes called the '''Arraby World Cup''' or simply '''the World Cup''', is an international [[Arraby]] competition contested by the senior men's national teams of the member associations of the [[FLLA]], the sport's global governing body. The tournament has been held every four years since [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700]] in its current world-wide form, having previously been staged from 1656 onwards as the Ayuman Continental Tournament. The most recent edition, the [[1764 FLLA World Cup]], was held in [[Raledria]] and won by [[Easuhura]], who defeated [[Emara]] 2–1 in the final at the Tirna National Stadium.

The competition's current format involves a qualification phase, in which national teams compete for places in the 32-team finals tournament. The host nation, or co-hosts, qualify automatically. The finals are held in a single host country (or, on three occasions, jointly across multiple host countries) over the course of approximately one month, with eight first-round groups followed by a knockout round culminating in the final. Twenty-four editions of the FLLA World Cup have been completed since 1656; on four further occasions, in 1664, 1688, 1692 and 1696, the planned tournament was cancelled because of intercontinental conflict. The next edition, the [[1768 FLLA World Cup|1768 World Cup]], will be held in [[Sanagara]].

Twelve different national teams have won the FLLA World Cup. [[Lycroa]] and [[Raledria]] are the most successful sides, each having claimed the trophy on four occasions; [[Emara]] has three titles and [[Praesyu]], [[Verusa]] and [[New Misos]] each have two. The remaining six champion nations, [[Estijan]], [[Eldjo]], [[Alzurian Union|Alzuria]], [[United Delet]], [[Quidic]] and [[Easuhura]], have lifted the trophy once each. National teams from the [[AFLA]], the Ayuman confederation, have between them won sixteen of the twenty-four completed editions.

==History==

===Origins (pre-1656)===

Organised international [[Arraby]] in the modern sense dates from the establishment of the Ayuman Football Federation, the predecessor of the [[AFLA]], by associations from [[Emara]], [[Lycroa]], [[Praesyu]] and [[Estijan]] in 1644. The first matches between national selections under the Federation's authority were played in 1647, but were arranged on an ad-hoc basis without a fixed competitive structure. The decision to organise a recurring continental tournament was taken at a Federation congress held in [[Huifarn]], [[Verusa]], in May 1654; the inaugural competition followed two years later.

The wider [[FLLA]] was constituted in 1683, formally extending the governance of Arraby beyond [[Ayuma]] by absorbing the older Ayuman Federation alongside emerging continental bodies in [[Atirha]] and [[New Ayre]]. The remaining four continental confederations, the [[EFLA]], [[QFLA]], [[MFLA]] and [[CFLA]], were admitted between 1685 and 1702.

===Continental Tournament (1656 to 1684)===

The first seven editions of the competition were contested under the title '''Ayuman Continental Tournament''', a designation reflecting the participation of teams drawn solely from the [[AFLA]] confederation. The inaugural [[1656 FLLA World Cup|1656 edition]] was hosted by [[Siana]] and contested by nine teams playing a straight knockout format; [[Estijan]] defeated [[Eldjo]] 4–2 in the final, a result remembered as the first major international honour won by an Estijan side. Four years later, the [[1660 FLLA World Cup|1660 edition]] in [[Easuhura]] produced the highest scoring final in the competition's history when [[Lycroa]] defeated [[Emara]] 6–1, a margin not surpassed at any subsequent edition.

The [[1664 FLLA World Cup|1664 tournament]], scheduled to be held in [[Kingdom of Alzuria|Alzuria]] with the largest field then contemplated (nine teams), was cancelled by the Federation's Council on 11 May 1661 following the outbreak of the [[Great Imperial War]]. The competition resumed in [[1668 FLLA World Cup|1668]] with [[Eldjo]] hosting twelve teams; the cycle continued without interruption through the [[1672 FLLA World Cup|1672]], [[1676 FLLA World Cup|1676]], [[1680 FLLA World Cup|1680]] and [[1684 FLLA World Cup|1684 editions]]. The 1680 final, contested between [[Lycroa]] and [[Eldjo]] at the Pyesion Stadium in [[Huetun]], finished goalless after extra time and was settled by a single coin toss, a method of resolution unique in the tournament's records.

===Red War cancellations (1688 to 1696)===

Three consecutive editions, those scheduled for [[1688 FLLA World Cup|1688]], [[1692 FLLA World Cup|1692]] and [[1696 FLLA World Cup|1696]], were cancelled as a result of the [[Red War]] (1688 to 1695) and the subsequent reconstruction. The 1688 tournament, awarded to [[Raledria]] at a Federation Congress in 1685, had reached the stage of stadium allocation and team registration before the outbreak of hostilities on 22 May 1688 forced its postponement and ultimate cancellation. The Federation Council subsequently determined, in resolutions of 1690 and 1694, that no tournament could be safely organised while widespread combat operations continued.

The cancelled cycle is the longest hiatus in the FLLA World Cup's history. It also coincided with the most significant restructuring of the international game: the Federation, reconstituted as the modern [[FLLA]] in 1683, used the war and post-war period to admit further continental bodies and to plan the worldwide expansion of its principal tournament.

===Rebranding and globalisation (1700 to 1736)===

The [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]], held in [[Raledria]] and won by the hosts, was the first to be styled the '''FLLA World Cup''', a change formally adopted by the FLLA Council on 14 February 1699. The rebranding reflected the participation of teams from all then-existing continental confederations and the Council's stated intention that subsequent editions be held outside [[Ayuma]] on a regular basis. The 1700 final, contested at the Tirna National Stadium, drew an estimated crowd of 38,000, the largest single-match attendance at any international fixture to that date.

The [[1704 FLLA World Cup|1704 edition]] returned to Ayuma but the [[1708 FLLA World Cup|1708 tournament]] became the first to be staged in [[New Ayre]], hosted by [[United Delet]] who also won the trophy on home soil. Successive editions through to the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]] alternated between Ayuman and non-Ayuman hosts in an informal rotation, though no fixed policy then governed the choice. The [[1716 FLLA World Cup|1716 edition]] was the subject of the first significant administrative controversy in the competition's history: the tournament had originally been awarded to [[Estijan]] in 1712, but the Estijan bid was withdrawn by the FLLA Council in November 1714 following the disclosure of a coordinated programme of performance-enhancing pharmaceutical use within the Estijan domestic league. The hosting rights passed to [[Easuhura]], who staged the tournament at four months' notice.

The [[1724 FLLA World Cup|1724 edition]] in [[Areoix Lie]], an [[Acrola|Acrolan]] nation, was the first held in [[Acrola]] and expanded the finals tournament to 24 teams. The expansion was rolled back, on cost grounds, for the [[1728 FLLA World Cup|1728 edition]] in [[Emara]] (16 teams) before being reinstated at the [[1732 FLLA World Cup|1732 tournament]] in [[Dahe]], the first FLLA World Cup held in [[Massir]].

===Expansion to 32 teams and the rotation policy (1740 to present)===

The [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]] in [[Seytinemas]] expanded the finals to the present figure of 32 teams, a change accompanied by the introduction of a four-pot seeded draw and a standardised group-stage format that has since remained substantially unchanged. The 1740 final, contested between [[New Misos]] and [[Lycroa]] at the Vulna Olympic Stadium, was the first to be broadcast by a transcontinental radio relay.

In 1742, two years after the format expansion, the FLLA Council adopted a formal '''confederation rotation policy''', under which the right to host the tournament passes between continental confederations in a fixed sequence. The policy was first applied to the selection of the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744]] hosts ([[Lycroa]], [[AFLA]]) and has been observed without exception since.

The [[1748 FLLA World Cup|1748 edition]] in [[New Misos]] (the second by an [[Atirha]]-hosted side) was won by the hosts and is widely described in FLLA literature as the "Greatest World Cup in History" on the strength of its goal-per-match average and the technical quality of the final. The [[1752 FLLA World Cup|1752 edition]] in [[United Delet]], the [[1756 FLLA World Cup|1756 tournament]] (the first held in [[Quia]], jointly hosted by [[Erkizil]], [[Quidic]], [[Wundry]] and [[Ztesh]]), the [[1760 FLLA World Cup|1760 edition]] in [[Ukhdari]] and the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 tournament]] in [[Raledria]] have followed the rotation in turn. The [[1768 FLLA World Cup|1768 edition]] was awarded to [[Sanagara]] at the FLLA Council meeting of 28 September 1764, returning the tournament to [[Massir]] for the first time since 1732.

==Trophy==

The current FLLA World Cup Trophy, presented to the winners of every edition since [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740]], is a 38-centimetre silver-and-gold sculpture depicting two stylised figures supporting a representation of the globe of [[Andah]]. The trophy was designed by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] sculptor Mariosa Calvelli following an international competition organised by the FLLA in 1738; the original is held at the [[FLLA]] headquarters in [[Tirna]] and the winning nation receives a gold-plated replica for permanent retention. The original was previously transferred to the winner of each edition until 1740, when the present custodial arrangement was adopted to safeguard the work.

The pre-1740 trophy, an older and substantially smaller piece styled the '''Ayuma Cup''', was used at the first eighteen editions of the tournament. The Ayuma Cup is now displayed at the Museum of Arraby in [[Huifarn]].

==Format==

===Qualification===

Qualification for the FLLA World Cup begins approximately three years before the finals tournament. The 32 places at the finals are distributed across the seven [[FLLA]] confederations on the basis of fixed allocations, adjusted by the FLLA Council in advance of each cycle. The current allocation, in force since 1740 and unchanged since 1756, is: four places to the [[NFLA]], five to the [[AFLA]], four to the [[NAFLA]], five to the [[EFLA]], four to the [[QFLA]], five to the [[MFLA]] and five to the [[CFLA]]. The host country, or each member of a co-host group, qualifies automatically and does not occupy a confederation slot. The reigning champions qualified automatically from 1740 until the rule was repealed in advance of the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]]; under amendments adopted by the FLLA Council in September 1764, the defending-champion exemption has been reinstated for the [[1768 FLLA World Cup|1768 cycle]].

Each confederation administers its own qualifying competition, with the format reflecting the size of its membership. [[NFLA]] qualification consists of first-round groups followed by a final octagonal round-robin. The [[AFLA]] runs five qualifying groups, the winners of which qualify directly. The [[NAFLA]] holds a single league-format competition of all its member nations. The [[EFLA]] divides its membership into five qualifying groups, the winners of which advance. The [[QFLA]] holds first-round groups followed by a two-group final round. The [[MFLA]] employs an identical format to the QFLA. The [[CFLA]] holds first-round groups followed by single-leg knockout playoffs.

===Final tournament===

The finals tournament, since 1740, has consisted of a group stage followed by a knockout round. Thirty-two teams are drawn into eight groups of four; each team plays the other three sides in its group in a single round-robin, with three points awarded for a win and one for a draw. The top two teams in each group advance to the knockout stage; the bottom two are eliminated. Tiebreakers between teams level on points are applied in the following order: goal difference, goals scored, head-to-head record, fair-play points, and, if necessary, a drawing of lots.

The knockout stage consists of single-elimination ties played over 90 minutes. Ties level at the end of normal time are extended by a 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]] of two 15-minute halves; if scores remain level after extra time, the tie is decided by [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]]. The two semi-final losers contest a third-place playoff on the day before the final.

The opening match, traditionally featuring the host nation, is played on the first day of the tournament. The final is played at the highest-capacity venue available in the host country, normally the same stadium as the opening match. From 1740 to 1764 inclusive, every final has been contested on the second Saturday of July.

[[Lycroa]] and [[Raledria]] share the record for most FLLA World Cup titles with four each. Lycroa, who lifted the trophy at the [[1660 FLLA World Cup|1660]], [[1680 FLLA World Cup|1680]], [[1732 FLLA World Cup|1732]] and [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744]] editions, are the only side to have won the competition in three different centuries of the [[Arten calendar]] and the most frequent finalist with seven appearances. Raledria are the only side to have lifted the trophy three times in succession, doing so at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700]], [[1712 FLLA World Cup|1712]] and [[1716 FLLA World Cup|1716]] editions; the run also marks the only occasion on which a side has won as host (1700), as a qualifier from a different continent (1712 in [[Praesyu]]), and as a continental visitor (1716 in [[Easuhura]]) in consecutive cycles.

Three nations have finished as runners-up at an FLLA World Cup without ever winning the tournament: [[Seytinemas]] (1748), [[Siana]] (1684 and 1704) and [[Taval]] (1728). A further set of nations, including [[United Delet]] (third in 1760) and [[Verusa]] (third in 1764), have reached the semi-finals at recent editions without progressing to the final.

===By confederation===

The sixteen titles won by [[AFLA]] (Ayuman) sides represent two-thirds of the twenty-four editions completed. The [[NFLA]] (Atirhan) confederation accounts for the next-largest share, with six titles. The remaining two completed editions were won by the [[NAFLA]] ([[New Ayre]]) at the [[1708 FLLA World Cup|1708 tournament]] and the [[QFLA]] ([[Quia]]) at the [[1756 FLLA World Cup|1756 tournament]]; the [[EFLA]] ([[Mahea]]), [[MFLA]] ([[Massir]]) and [[CFLA]] ([[Acrola]]) have not produced a champion to date, although all three confederations have provided host nations.

The [[AFLA]] confederation also accounts for the largest share of finals contested: across the twenty-four completed editions, an Ayuman side has appeared in the final on twenty occasions, with fourteen of those finals contested between two Ayuman sides.

===Host performance===

Ten of the twenty-four completed editions have been won by the host nation. The home-winning sides are [[Emara]] (1672), [[Lycroa]] (1680), [[Alzurian Union]] (1684), [[Raledria]] (1700), [[Emara]] again (1704), [[United Delet]] (1708), [[Emara]] for a third time (1728), [[Lycroa]] for a second time (1744), [[New Misos]] (1748) and [[Quidic]] (1756, as a member of the four-nation [[Quia]] co-host group). No host has lifted the trophy at home since 1756. Of the two subsequent contested editions, the hosts [[Ukhdari]] were eliminated in the round of sixteen at [[1760 FLLA World Cup|1760]] and [[Raledria]] in the quarter-finals at [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764]], neither nation progressing beyond the quarter-finals on home soil.

The hosts of the [[1664 FLLA World Cup|1664]], [[1688 FLLA World Cup|1688]], [[1692 FLLA World Cup|1692]] and [[1696 FLLA World Cup|1696]] editions, awarded but not contested because of intercontinental conflict, do not count towards this statistic.

==Awards==

The FLLA presents six awards at the conclusion of each finals tournament:

* The '''FLLA Golden Ball''', awarded by a panel of sports journalists to the best player of the tournament. The current holder is [[Easuhura|Easuhuran]] central midfielder Sahel Mavari, who received the award at the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]].
* The '''FLLA Golden Boot''', awarded to the tournament's top goalscorer; current holder Theio Ravar of [[Emara]] won the prize at the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]] with nine personal strikes.
* The '''FLLA Golden Glove''', awarded to the best goalkeeper of the tournament; current holder Niran Yokima of [[Easuhura]] received the award at the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]].
* The '''FLLA Best Young Player Award''', awarded to the leading performer aged 21 or under at the start of the tournament; current holder Anders Vellholm of [[Verusa]], 19 at the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]], received the award.
* The '''FLLA Fair Play Trophy''', awarded to the team finishing the tournament with the fewest disciplinary points; current holders are [[Seytinemas]].
* The '''Leading Goalscoring Nation''' award, presented to the side that scored the most goals across all of its matches at the tournament; current holders are [[Emara]] with 17 goals at the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]].

The Golden Ball, Boot and Glove have been presented in their current form since 1744; the Best Young Player Award was added in 1752 and the Fair Play Trophy in 1756.

==Symbols==

===Emblem and trophy===

Each edition of the FLLA World Cup adopts its own official emblem, designed in advance of the tournament by a creative agency commissioned by the host association. The series of emblems is regulated by the FLLA's Marketing Directorate, which issues guidelines on typography, colour and visual treatment in advance of each cycle. The host nation's flag is by convention incorporated into the design of the emblem.

The trophy itself, the present FLLA World Cup Trophy ([[#Trophy|see above]]), is the universal visual symbol of the competition and appears in stylised form on most modern editions' emblems.

===Mascot===

Since the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]] the host association has selected an official mascot, normally an anthropomorphic representation of a culturally significant animal of the host country. Mascots are now selected by public vote organised by the host association approximately two years before the tournament. The mascot of the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]] was Vanara, a stylised silver syaral; the [[1760 FLLA World Cup|1760 mascot]] was Falir, an anthropomorphic Ukhdari falcon.

===Match ball===

A bespoke match ball is manufactured for each edition of the tournament, normally by a sporting-goods manufacturer based in the host country. The ball is named and branded for the edition; the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 ball]] was the Tirneza, a 14-panel thermally-bonded ball that succeeded the traditional 32-panel hand-stitched construction used at every earlier edition since 1740.

==Media and sponsorship==

The FLLA World Cup is one of the most-watched sporting events in the world. The [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]] was broadcast in 187 countries and is reported by the FLLA to have drawn a cumulative live broadcast audience of 3.9 billion individual viewers across all matches, with 1.8 billion individuals tuning in to at least part of the final. The Marketing Directorate of the FLLA administers the worldwide commercial programme for the tournament, structured since the [[1756 FLLA World Cup|1756 edition]] as a tiered sponsorship hierarchy of six worldwide partners, eight national partners and four to six regional supporters.

Total sponsorship revenue across the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 cycle]] was {{lahn}}1.45&nbsp;billion, the highest figure recorded by any FLLA World Cup to that date. Total tournament revenue at the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]], audited by the FLLA in August 1764, was {{lahn}}5.91&nbsp;billion; a share of this revenue is returned to the host association under the FLLA's 18 per cent host-allocation rule, the remainder financing the FLLA's worldwide development programmes and its administrative operations.

==Notable matches and controversies==

The following are among the most frequently discussed individual matches in the history of the FLLA World Cup:

* The '''[[1656 FLLA World Cup|1656 final]]''', the first international fixture decided under standardised Federation rules, in which [[Estijan]] beat [[Eldjo]] 4–2.
* The '''[[1680 FLLA World Cup|1680 final]]''', the only final in the tournament's history to have been decided by a coin toss after a goalless 120 minutes between [[Lycroa]] and [[Eldjo]].
* The '''[[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 final]]''', the first edition of the tournament held under the "World Cup" name, won by [[Raledria]] against [[United Delet]].
* The '''[[1716 FLLA World Cup|1716 hosting controversy]]''', in which the tournament was reallocated from [[Estijan]] to [[Easuhura]] on the disclosure of a coordinated programme of performance-enhancing pharmaceutical use within the Estijan domestic league.
* The '''[[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 final]]''', remembered for an unusual incident in which the floodlights at the host stadium failed for thirty-six minutes during the second half.
* The '''[[1748 FLLA World Cup|1748 final]]''', widely described in FLLA literature as the most technically distinguished match in the competition's history.
* '''The Miracle of Rovik''' at the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 quarter-finals]], in which the eventual champions [[Easuhura]] eliminated host nation [[Raledria]] 1–0 from an attacking move that Raledrian replays subsequently suggested had begun from an offside position. The Raledrian Arraby Association lodged a formal protest, which the FLLA Disciplinary Committee declined to entertain.
